art.alt: An engraved transistor lattice rising through computational layers into a neural graph
art.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: wide 16:9 editorial series plate for a serious long-form knowledge garden
Primary request: depict the foundations of computing as one continuous ascent: a precise transistor lattice and silicon-gate geometry in the lower foreground, rising through stacked circuit and abstraction layers, then resolving into a sparse neural-network graph in the upper field
Scene/backdrop: warm cream archival paper, open margins, no literal interface or screen
Style/medium: tactile copperplate engraving and restrained linocut marks, overlaid with translucent technical-vellum layers and fine drafting lines; intellectually serious editorial illustration, materially believable, hand-made precision
Composition/framing: panoramic 16:9; grounded transistor lattice across the lower third, layered upward progression through the middle, neural graph opening into the upper third; balanced asymmetry and generous breathing room
Lighting/mood: quiet, lucid, contemplative; no theatrical lighting
Color palette: cream paper, charcoal ink, oxide red, with one restrained cobalt-blue accent
Materials/textures: subtle paper grain, etched metal lines, translucent vellum, faint registration imperfections
Constraints: textless; no letters, numbers, labels, code glyphs, logos, signatures, or watermark; visual relationships must remain legible at banner size
Avoid: generic sci-fi glow, neon, cyberpunk, glossy 3D, humanoid robots, brains, floating UI panels, decorative clutter

visuals.title: The tower, grouped into six handholds
visuals.caption: Each group hides mechanisms below by making a precise promise to the groups above.

items.label: Physics
items.detail: Doped silicon supplies reliably distinguishable voltage states.

items.label: Switch
items.detail: A transistor turns an electrical signal into controllable on or off.

items.label: Logic
items.detail: Gates and circuits compose switches into add, compare, store, and select.

items.label: Processor
items.detail: The ISA exposes a documented vocabulary of instructions above billions of transistors.

items.label: Language
items.detail: Assembly and high-level syntax let people state work without handling the circuitry.

items.label: Application
items.detail: The browser, spreadsheet, or model reduces the tower to an action a person can take.

visuals.title: Ride 2 + 3 all the way down
visuals.caption: The answer survives every translation even though no layer understands addition.

items.label: Python
items.detail: The high-level expression asks the language runtime to produce 5.

items.label: Bytecode
items.detail: The operation becomes load, load, add, and store instructions.

items.label: Machine code
items.detail: The interpreter ultimately executes the processor's add instruction.

items.label: Bits
items.detail: The operands arrive as 0010 and 0011 and leave as 0101.

items.label: Gates
items.detail: XOR produces sum digits while AND produces carries.

items.label: Transistors
items.detail: Gate voltages open and close channels a few nanometers wide.

visuals.title: One machine can simulate any Turing machine you can describe
visuals.caption: Turing's universal-machine idea separates the fixed mechanism from the behavior encoded on its tape.

items.label: Describe
items.detail: Write another machine's states and rules as symbols rather than rebuilding its hardware.

items.label: Load
items.detail: Place that description beside the other machine's input on the universal machine's tape.

items.label: Interpret
items.detail: A fixed rule table reads the description and reproduces the described machine step by step.

items.label: Become
items.detail: Change the stored bits and the same physical machine behaves as a spreadsheet, game, map, or piano.

visuals.title: Programming moves away from the machine
visuals.caption: Every rung makes human intent easier to state and gives the machine more translation work.

items.label: Note G
items.detail: Ada Lovelace specifies the Analytical Engine's Bernoulli-number operations on paper.

items.label: Plugboards
items.detail: ENIAC programs are physical arrangements of switches and cables.

items.label: A-0
items.detail: Grace Hopper's translator assembles subroutine calls into a runnable program.

items.label: FORTRAN
items.detail: A mainstream high-level language lets formulas stand in for assembly.

items.label: Language bloom
items.detail: Lisp treats programs as data, C stays close to the machine, and SQL states goals.

items.label: Plain language
items.detail: Instructions given to a language model extend the same abstraction climb.

visuals.title: Three grammars, one answer
visuals.caption: The sum of the squares of the even numbers from 1 through 10 is 220 in every grammar.

items.label: Imperative
items.detail: Mutate a running total with explicit loop and condition steps.

items.label: Functional
items.detail: Express a pipeline that filters, squares, and sums without mutation.

items.label: Declarative
items.detail: State the desired rows and aggregation, then let the SQL engine plan the procedure.

visuals.title: The text is a snapshot of a larger theory
visuals.caption: A codebase stays healthy when the people changing it can connect the written artifact back to the problem it was built to solve.

items.label: Problem
items.detail: The real domain supplies needs, constraints, edge cases, and reasons for making the system.

items.label: Team theory
items.detail: Programmers hold a working account of how the pieces answer that problem and which changes are safe.

items.label: Source text
items.detail: Code records part of that account precisely enough for a machine, but not all of its reasons.

items.label: Handoff
items.detail: When the theory does not travel with the text, a new team can preserve every character and still make the system rot.

visuals.title: Text becomes behavior one artifact at a time
visuals.caption: A compiler pipeline hands a concrete intermediate artifact from each specialist stage to the next.

items.label: Lex
items.detail: Source characters become tokens with names and boundaries.

items.label: Parse
items.detail: Tokens become a typed syntax tree with grammatical structure.

items.label: Lower
items.detail: The tree becomes intermediate representation in the compiler's own language.

items.label: Optimize
items.detail: IR is rewritten into equivalent IR that says the same thing better.

items.label: Generate
items.detail: The target machine's instructions become assembly and then an object file.

items.label: Link
items.detail: Objects and libraries resolve their symbol IOUs into one executable.

visuals.title: A backdoor that survives clean source
visuals.caption: Ken Thompson's attack moves the malicious rule from inspectable source into the self-reproducing compiler binary.

items.label: Recognition
items.detail: The compiler recognizes when it is compiling the login program.

items.label: Insertion
items.detail: It silently inserts a login backdoor into the produced binary.

items.label: Self-recognition
items.detail: The compiler also recognizes when it is compiling its own source.

items.label: Reproduction
items.detail: It inserts both recognition tricks into the next compiler binary.

items.label: Clean source
items.detail: The malicious source is removed while the binary keeps propagating the behavior.

visuals.title: From stack traffic to a compile-time 144
visuals.caption: The compiler can erase the structure you wrote only when each rewrite preserves the program's meaning.

items.label: Start
items.detail: Unoptimized IR stores the argument in a stack slot, loads it twice, multiplies, then returns.

items.label: Promote
items.detail: The mem2reg pass proves the stack slot is unnecessary and reduces the function to multiply and return.

items.label: Inline
items.detail: At the call site, the optimizer substitutes the body of square for the call square(12).

items.label: Fold
items.detail: With both operands known, it computes 12 × 12 during compilation and emits the constant 144.

items.label: Obligation
items.detail: Every disappearance is safe only because a pass proved the replacement equivalent.

visuals.title: The bend between the matrices
visuals.caption: Without a nonlinear twist, any depth of matrix multiplications collapses into one matrix.

items.label: Matrix A
items.detail: The first learned linear map stretches, rotates, or mixes the incoming vector.

items.label: Matrix B
items.detail: A second linear map still composes exactly with the first.

items.label: Collapse
items.detail: A thousand linear layers equal one product matrix and buy no new kind of boundary.

items.label: Nonlinearity
items.detail: A ReLU-style bend blocks the collapse and makes composition expressive.

visuals.title: Where to look, what to move
visuals.caption: An attention head turns pairwise similarities into a budget for moving information between token vectors.

items.label: Project
items.detail: Learned matrices turn each token into query, key, and value vectors.

items.label: Score
items.detail: Each query takes a dot product with the available keys.

items.label: Scale
items.detail: Scores are divided by the square root of the head dimension.

items.label: Budget
items.detail: Softmax makes positive weights whose row sums exactly to one.

items.label: Move
items.detail: The weighted value average is projected back into the token's running representation.

visuals.title: A projection keeps one view and discards the rest
visuals.caption: An attention head reads a high-dimensional token through a learned low-rank bottleneck rather than seeing every direction equally.

items.label: Full space
items.detail: A GPT-2-small token arrives as one point in a 768-dimensional representation space.

items.label: Learned question
items.detail: A projection selects the combinations of directions useful to this particular head.

items.label: Rank-64 shadow
items.detail: The 768-dimensional input is compressed into a 64-dimensional query, key, or value vector.

items.label: Deliberate loss
items.detail: Most directions disappear from this view; the bottleneck forces the head to summarize.

visuals.title: A weighted vote with one bend
visuals.caption: The smallest neural unit is a short arithmetic path, not a miniature biological mind.

items.label: Inputs
items.detail: Numbers arrive from data or from neurons in the previous layer.

items.label: Weights
items.detail: Each stored multiplier says how strongly and in which direction an input matters.

items.label: Bias
items.detail: One learned offset shifts the point at which the unit responds strongly.

items.label: Sum
items.detail: Weighted inputs and the bias combine into one pre-activation value.

items.label: Activation
items.detail: A nonlinear rule such as ReLU bends the result so stacked layers do not collapse.

visuals.title: Forward, compare, backward, nudge
visuals.caption: The toy network exposes the same training skeleton used at frontier scale.

items.label: Forward
items.detail: Two hidden ReLU units produce a prediction of 0.5 for a target of 1.

items.label: Measure
items.detail: Half squared error makes the starting loss 0.125.

items.label: Backward
items.detail: The output error flows through the old weights to produce every gradient.

items.label: Update
items.detail: Each weight steps against its gradient with learning rate 0.1.

items.label: Replay
items.detail: The new prediction is 1.16875 and the loss falls to about 0.0142.

visuals.title: One straight boundary fails; a hidden layer changes the geometry
visuals.caption: XOR shows both the exact limit of a single-layer perceptron and the precise reason depth first mattered.

items.label: Four cases
items.detail: XOR labels the two points on one diagonal 1 and the two points on the other diagonal 0.

items.label: One layer
items.detail: A single perceptron draws one straight decision boundary, and no line separates those diagonals.

items.label: Hidden layer
items.detail: Intermediate neurons can combine multiple straight boundaries into a region that separates XOR.

items.label: Honest theorem
items.detail: Universal approximation establishes expressiveness in principle, not easy training, compact size, or the right weights.

visuals.title: Turn wrongness into a direction
visuals.caption: Differentiable learning repeats a loop that uses local slope to seek lower loss; stochasticity or an oversized step can still push one update uphill.

items.label: Data
items.detail: Training examples pair the inputs with the outputs the task should produce.

items.label: Model
items.detail: A chosen family of functions exposes adjustable parameters.

items.label: Predict
items.detail: The current parameter setting produces outputs on the examples.

items.label: Loss
items.detail: One number measures how wrong those outputs are.

items.label: Gradient
items.detail: Calculus identifies the local direction that increases the loss fastest.

items.label: Nudge
items.detail: Parameters step against that direction and the cycle begins again.

visuals.title: Match the family's bias to the shape of the problem
visuals.caption: No family wins everywhere because every method assumes a different structure in the world.

items.label: Linear
items.detail: Flat relationships reward interpretability and work well as a baseline.

items.label: Nearest neighbors
items.detail: Nearby inputs are assumed to deserve nearby answers.

items.label: Trees
items.detail: Sharp feature thresholds carve tabular data into readable regions.

items.label: Ensembles
items.detail: Many trees average or repair one another on rows-and-columns problems.

items.label: SVMs
items.detail: A widest-margin boundary suits medium data with separable classes.

items.label: Neural networks
items.detail: Hierarchical learned features dominate raw perception and language at scale.

visuals.title: Four doors between fitting and trust
visuals.caption: A model earns evidence of generalization only when each later dataset remains untouched by the decisions made at the earlier one.

items.label: Train
items.detail: Fit parameters on the examples the learner is allowed to see, even if training error reaches zero.

items.label: Validate
items.detail: Choose architectures and settings on a separate slice so those decisions do not consume the final test.

items.label: Test once
items.detail: Use the untouched test set for the final same-distribution estimate, not as an iterative steering signal.

items.label: Meet the world
items.detail: Deployment can still shift hospitals, economies, sensors, or adversaries beyond what any held-out split promised.

visuals.title: Parts become wholes as depth accumulates
visuals.caption: A trained vision network reuses simple early features to assemble increasingly specific representations.

items.label: Edges
items.detail: Early layers respond to oriented edges and color blobs.

items.label: Textures
items.detail: Middle layers combine edges into textures, corners, and simple motifs.

items.label: Parts
items.detail: Deeper layers assemble motifs into an eye, a wheel, or a beak.

items.label: Objects
items.detail: Final layers integrate reusable parts into whole-object representations.

visuals.title: Each solution becomes the next wall
visuals.caption: The field advances by scaling a new axis until the bottleneck shifts again.

items.label: Depth
items.detail: AlexNet and ResNet bypass vanishing gradients with ReLU and residuals.

items.label: Sequences
items.detail: Transformers pair attention with self-supervised next-token data.

items.label: Model + data
items.detail: Chinchilla-style training scales parameters and tokens together.

items.label: Deliberation
items.detail: Reasoning models add inference-time compute as another axis.

visuals.title: Nearly the same compute, a different allocation
visuals.caption: The comparison showed that frontier models of the period were spending too much of a fixed training budget on parameters and too little on data.

items.label: Gopher
items.detail: 280 billion parameters × 300 billion tokens × 6 gives about 5.0 × 10²³ training FLOP.

items.label: Chinchilla
items.detail: 70 billion parameters × 1.4 trillion tokens × 6 gives about 5.9 × 10²³ training FLOP.

items.label: Reallocation
items.detail: One-quarter the parameters and about 4.7 times the data produced the stronger benchmark result.

items.label: Rule of thumb
items.detail: The 1.4-trillion-to-70-billion ratio is 20 training tokens per parameter for that measured regime.

visuals.title: The same gradient, three journeys
visuals.caption: Learning rate controls whether the optimizer crosses the landscape, explodes across it, or barely moves.

items.label: Too large
items.detail: Steps overshoot the valley and the loss can climb toward divergence.

items.label: Usable
items.detail: Steps move downhill while remaining small enough to correct course.

items.label: Too small
items.detail: Training still works locally but takes geologic time and expensive compute.

visuals.title: Six patches on difficult geometry
visuals.caption: Each optimizer adds memory or structure to make a noisy downhill path more effective.

items.label: SGD
items.detail: Step on an unbiased noisy minibatch gradient.

items.label: Momentum
items.detail: Average recent gradients so bouncing cancels and consistent motion accumulates.

items.label: RMSProp
items.detail: Adapt each weight's step to its history of gradient scale.

items.label: Adam
items.detail: Combine momentum, per-weight scale, and early-step bias correction.

items.label: AdamW
items.detail: Decouple weight decay from Adam's adaptive update.

items.label: Muon
items.detail: Treat updates as matrices and equalize strength across their directions.

visuals.title: Two fast corrections, then a long shallow crawl
visuals.caption: Fitting y = 2x + 1 with two parameters makes difficult optimization geometry visible without hiding any arithmetic.

items.label: Blank model
items.detail: Start w = 0 and b = 0; predictions are zero and the first gradients are −22.667 and −10.

items.label: Overshoot
items.detail: The first update jumps to w = 2.267 and b = 1.0, already across the true slope.

items.label: Correct
items.detail: The next update pulls back to w = 2.018 and b = 0.893.

items.label: Creep
items.detail: The steep direction is settled, but the shallow direction leaves w = 2.0039 and b = 0.9912.

items.label: Converge
items.detail: Repeated small updates finally recover w = 2 and b = 1 to the printed precision.

visuals.title: Capability is built, then behavior is shaped
visuals.caption: Successive training regimes alter the same weights with different data, judges, and objectives.

items.label: Pretraining
items.detail: Trillions of next-token examples build a base model that can continue many kinds of text.

items.label: Instruction tuning
items.detail: Curated demonstrations select the conversational pattern of answering a user.

items.label: Preference tuning
items.detail: Human or AI comparisons push responses toward preferred behavior.

items.label: Reasoning RL
items.detail: Verifiable rewards can develop self-checking and longer reasoning strategies.

visuals.title: Three methods, one safety target
visuals.caption: Constitutional AI, DPO, and RLVR differ in how judgment reaches the model; safety is a target pursued through those tools, not a fourth algorithm.

items.label: Constitutional AI
items.detail: A written principle set guides self-critique, revision, and AI feedback.

items.label: DPO
items.detail: Preference pairs train the language model directly without a separate PPO loop.

items.label: RLVR
items.detail: Answer keys or test suites provide checkable rewards for reasoning.

items.label: Safety training
items.detail: Demonstrations and preferences teach when the model should not help.

visuals.title: Completion is not yet conversation
visuals.caption: A small local comparison isolates the behavioral difference post-training selects without claiming that every underlying capability changed.

items.label: Raw prompt
items.detail: Both models receive the question, “What is the capital of France?”

items.label: GPT-2 base
items.detail: A pretrained-only model may answer, continue with more questions, or drift because its job is plausible text continuation.

items.label: Instruct model
items.detail: A post-trained chat model, invoked through a role template, answers Paris directly and consistently.

items.label: Boundary
items.detail: The contrast demonstrates selected conversational behavior; it does not prove every capability or refusal sits unchanged underneath.

visuals.title: The chip is only the bottom layer
visuals.caption: NVIDIA's advantage compounds through a software stack that makes its parallel hardware usable and familiar.

items.label: GPU
items.detail: Thousands of simple processors execute the same small computation in parallel.

items.label: CUDA
items.detail: Ordinary C-like kernels expose general computation on the graphics hardware.

items.label: Libraries
items.detail: cuDNN, cuBLAS, NCCL, and TensorRT package recurring work.

items.label: Frameworks
items.detail: PyTorch and TensorFlow were built around the CUDA path.

items.label: Habit
items.detail: Millions of developers and research repositories assume the accumulated ecosystem.

visuals.title: Compute waits for memory
visuals.caption: Large-model performance depends on moving weights into arithmetic units, not merely owning more arithmetic units.

items.label: Weights
items.detail: Billions of stored parameters must be streamed for token generation.

items.label: HBM
items.detail: Vertically stacked memory sits millimeters from the accelerator.

items.label: Bandwidth
items.detail: Bytes per second increasingly determine whether compute units stay fed.

items.label: Compute array
items.detail: Multiply-accumulate units turn the arriving values into matrix operations.

items.label: Supply chain
items.detail: TSMC fabricates, memory suppliers provide HBM, and advanced packaging joins the system.

visuals.title: Turn a power headline into racks, chips, and capital
visuals.caption: This is an order-of-magnitude conversion with every soft assumption left visible rather than a bill of materials.

items.label: Campus
items.detail: Begin with a 1-gigawatt site and assume power-usage effectiveness of about 1.25.

items.label: Racks
items.detail: About 800 megawatts reaches equipment; at 130 kilowatts per NVL72 rack, that is roughly 6,100 racks.

items.label: GPUs
items.detail: Seventy-two GPUs per rack turns that rack count into roughly 440,000 accelerators.

items.label: Hardware
items.detail: At the stated soft street estimate of $3 million per rack, the accelerator hardware alone is about $18 billion.

items.label: Constraint
items.detail: Buildings, networking, cooling, substations, and grid queues move the bottleneck from chips toward electricity.

visuals.title: Three leading-edge manufacturers, one indispensable toolmaker
visuals.caption: The leading edge is concentrated in four firms and a handful of places.

items.label: TSMC
items.detail: Taiwan's foundry entered volume production of its N2 generation in late 2025.

items.label: Samsung
items.detail: South Korea's manufacturer is the second gate-all-around 2nm contender.

items.label: Intel
items.detail: Arizona's Fab 52 brought the 18A generation into mass production.

items.label: ASML
items.detail: The Dutch company alone supplies production-scale EUV tools used at the frontier.

visuals.title: An embargo acts as a brake, a leak, and a subsidy
visuals.caption: The control regime slows access while inducing substitution and creating pressure for evasive supply routes.

items.label: EUV blocked
items.detail: Dutch licensing under US pressure keeps EUV systems out of China.

items.label: Frontier chips blocked
items.detail: US rules deny top accelerators and advanced tools, prompting a weakened H20 design.

items.label: Policy whiplash
items.detail: H20 access is blocked, reopened, and followed by a proposed H200 opening.

items.label: Conditional licenses
items.detail: H200 sales become case-by-case with certification and a tariff.

items.label: Substitution
items.detail: SMIC uses costly DUV multi-patterning while Huawei's ecosystem gains a protected home market.

items.label: Leakage
items.detail: Teardowns reveal TSMC dies obtained through an intermediary before the route closed.

visuals.title: A five-stop verification chain for chip claims
visuals.caption: A smaller marketing number names an intended process generation; evidence about the actual product comes from architecture, production, and measurement.

items.label: Strip the label
items.detail: Treat N2, 18A, and SF2 as generation names, not literal measurements of one physical feature.

items.label: Name the change
items.detail: Ask whether the process changes transistor geometry, power delivery, density, or packaging.

items.label: Check production
items.detail: Use earnings-call records to distinguish a pilot announcement from high-volume manufacturing and revenue.

items.label: Check the silicon
items.detail: Use teardown measurements and die photographs for pitches, structures, provenance, and what actually shipped.

items.label: Check the board
items.detail: Use independent foundry-share data and the toolmaker's annual report for market and lithography claims.

visuals.title: How one foreign atom makes a switch possible
visuals.caption: Doping gives silicon mobile carriers, and their boundary creates a controllable electrical barrier.

items.label: Pure silicon
items.detail: Four outer electrons per atom are committed to four crystal bonds.

items.label: Add phosphorus
items.detail: A fifth outer electron has no bond and becomes a loose negative carrier.

items.label: Make n-type
items.detail: A sparse population of phosphorus creates electron-rich silicon.

items.label: Add boron
items.detail: One missing bond behaves as a mobile positive hole, making p-type silicon.

items.label: Join p and n
items.detail: Electrons fill nearby holes and leave a charge-depleted one-way barrier.

visuals.title: A chip is printed layer by layer
visuals.caption: The same patterned-wafer cycle builds both the devices and the wiring between them.

items.label: Slice
items.detail: A cylinder of pure silicon is cut into wafers.

items.label: Coat
items.detail: A light-sensitive chemical covers the wafer surface.

items.label: Expose
items.detail: Light projects one mask pattern onto the resist; EUV systems do this with mirrors rather than transmissive lenses.

items.label: Develop
items.detail: Changed or unchanged resist is washed away to open selected regions.

items.label: Modify
items.detail: The openings guide etching, dopant implantation, or material deposition.

items.label: Repeat
items.detail: Dozens of aligned patterned layers accumulate over months in the fab.

visuals.title: Moore's observation survives a back-of-the-envelope check
visuals.caption: Two documented transistor counts reproduce the famous two-year doubling pace while leaving clear that it was an industrial trend, not a physical law.

items.detail: Intel's first commercial microprocessor carried 2,300 transistors.

items.label: Blackwell die
items.detail: One NVIDIA Blackwell compute die carries about 104 billion transistors.

items.label: Growth
items.detail: 104 billion divided by 2,300 is about 45.2 million times.

items.label: Doublings
items.detail: The base-two logarithm of that growth is about 25.4 doublings.

items.label: Pace
items.detail: Fifty-three years divided by 25.4 gives about 2.1 years per doubling.

items.label: Boundary
items.detail: The result describes coordinated scaling history; today's “2 nm” remains a generation label, not a measured 2-nanometer feature.

visuals.title: Six disciplines for where to look next
visuals.caption: Classical algorithm families reuse a small set of strategies across otherwise different problems.

items.label: Divide and conquer
items.detail: Split the problem, solve smaller pieces, then combine them.

items.label: Greedy
items.detail: Take the locally best step and never revisit it.

items.label: Dynamic programming
items.detail: Store solved subproblems so no result is computed twice.

items.label: Graph traversal
items.detail: Walk a network systematically from node to node.

items.label: Randomized
items.detail: Use controlled coin flips for speed or estimation.

items.label: Backtracking
items.detail: Try a branch, detect failure, undo, and try another.

visuals.title: Proof for capability
visuals.caption: Written algorithms articulate every step; learned systems discover useful weight configurations without legible instructions.

items.label: Source
items.detail: A person writes explicit steps; a learned system receives data, a loss, and an optimizer.

items.label: Correctness
items.detail: The written procedure can carry an all-input theorem; the network carries a dated test score.

items.label: Failure
items.detail: A code bug may live on one line; a learned error is diffuse across weights and data.

items.label: Transfer
items.detail: Classical software is rewritten by hand; learned behavior may be redirected by fine-tuning.

visuals.title: The answer stays fixed while the remainder shrinks
visuals.caption: Three divisions expose the classical algorithmic ideal: every step is inspectable, termination is proved, and correctness is preserved.

items.label: First remainder
items.detail: 1071 = 2 × 462 + 147, so any common divisor of the original pair also divides 147.

items.label: Second remainder
items.detail: 462 = 3 × 147 + 21; replace the larger pair with the smaller pair without changing the gcd.

items.label: Stop
items.detail: 147 = 7 × 21 + 0; a remainder of zero makes the last nonzero remainder, 21, the answer.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: 1071 = 21 × 51 and 462 = 21 × 22, while 51 and 22 share no factor.

items.label: Proof shape
items.detail: Nonnegative remainders strictly decrease, so the procedure must terminate rather than merely seeming to.

visuals.title: Four layers inside one convenient call
visuals.caption: An SDK hides transport plumbing while the API contract remains the service's actual promise.

items.label: Your program
items.detail: Application code asks for an operation in its own language.

items.label: SDK
items.detail: The installed phrasebook serializes data, retries, parses, and streams.

items.label: HTTP
items.detail: Requests and responses carry the exchange across the network.

items.label: API contract
items.detail: Endpoints, fields, limits, and errors define what the remote service promises.

visuals.title: Four ways an interface carries its past
visuals.caption: Versioning strategies differ mainly in who must absorb the cost of change.

items.label: Semantic
items.detail: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tells library users when they must manage a breaking upgrade.

items.label: Date-pinned
items.detail: The provider preserves each account's older response shape for years.

items.label: URL version
items.detail: Parallel paths such as v1 and v2 share the migration burden.

items.label: No policy
items.detail: Users absorb continual breakage until ecosystem trust erodes.

visuals.title: An API contract includes its limits and failures
visuals.caption: One GitHub request makes the five recurring parts of an API promise visible without an SDK hiding them.

items.label: Address
items.detail: The repository URL turns one resource into a question a program can ask.

items.label: Status
items.detail: HTTP 200 says the request succeeded; a nonexistent repository returns 404.

items.label: Limits
items.detail: Rate-limit headers expose how much unauthenticated capacity remains and when identity changes the allowance.

items.label: Version
items.detail: A response header tells you which dated contract GitHub selected when you did not name one.

items.label: Shape
items.detail: Success returns documented JSON fields; failure returns a machine-readable message and documentation link.
